phase1.intro:
Before Java 7, closing a resource meant a finally block with a null check and its own nested try-catch. try-with-resources replaces all of that with one line.

Where do you want to start?

dialogue: Declare the resource right inside the try's parentheses — `try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(...)) { ... }` — and [[key:Java automatically calls close() on it for you the moment the block ends]], whether it ended normally or via exception.
No finally, no null check, no nested try-catch for the close() call itself.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔚 auto-closes when the block ends, no matter what
stickyNote.definition: try (Resource r = ...) { ... } automatically calls close() on r when the block ends, normally or via exception.

topics.buttonText: Can I close more than one resource this way?
dialogue: You can declare more than one resource in the same parentheses, separated by semicolons, and [[key:they close in the REVERSE order they were opened]] — the last one declared is the first one closed.

stickyNote.definition: Multiple resources in one try-with-resources close in reverse order of declaration — the last declared closes first.

topics.buttonText: What does something need to work in try-with-resources?
dialogue: [[warn:Whatever you put in those parentheses has to implement AutoCloseable]] (or its older cousin, Closeable). BufferedReader, Scanner, FileWriter already do — and implementing AutoCloseable yourself is just writing one close() method.

stickyNote.flavor: ✅ one close() method to join the club
stickyNote.definition: Only classes implementing AutoCloseable (or Closeable) can be used in try-with-resources — implementing it means writing one close() method.

phase2.errorMessage:
Test.java:6: error: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to AutoCloseable
        try (String s = "Hello") {  // String doesn't implement AutoCloseable!
            ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
try (String s = "Hello") { ... } looks like it should work — it's the same syntax — but String doesn't implement AutoCloseable. There's no close() method on String at all, so Java has nothing to call when the block ends, and refuses to compile rather than silently do nothing.

[[key:try-with-resources only accepts objects that implement AutoCloseable]] — that's not a suggestion, it's a hard requirement enforced at compile time, same as any other interface implementation check.

If you genuinely just need a value inside a try block without any cleanup behavior, that's what a normal try (or even just a regular variable outside the try) is for — try-with-resources specifically exists for things that NEED closing.
phase2.openingDialogue: Watch what happens when a value doesn't know how to close~

phase3.openingDialogue: Let's build a resource that knows how to clean up after itself~

mcq.question:
Which statement about try-with-resources is TRUE?

A) Any class can be used inside try-with-resources, no interface required
B) Resources are closed in the same order they were declared
C) A resource used in try-with-resources must implement AutoCloseable
D) try-with-resources removes the need for a catch block entirely

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Uses try-with-resources to create a Scanner reading from a file called "data.txt"
2. Reads and prints all lines from the file
3. Catches IOException if file not found

Note: For this exercise, assume the file exists with some sample text.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: try-with-resources was added in Java 7 (2011) — meaning for over 15 years, every Java developer had to write the manual finally-with-null-check pattern by hand. It's one of the clearer examples of a language feature that didn't add new capability so much as remove an entire category of resource-leak bugs that used to be extremely common in real Java codebases.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~
